steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Even if you have to pay more and even if you would never follow through on making a warranty claim if your pan broke, you should only buy a pan that has a warranty.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: If offering a warranty meant that a company would need to reimburse a bunch of customers when the product broke, then manufacturers wouldn't offer a warranty.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This premise is conditional. By contrapositive, it tells us something about every frying pan that comes with a warranty.
```
manufacturer offers a warranty  →  manufacturer does not expect to reimburse many customers
```
So the author says we should only buy pans with a warranty, because a warranty means the manufacturer is not worried about paying out a lot of claims.

The author assumes the manufacturer is not worried because the pan is good: it is not expected to fail for many buyers.

But maybe the manufacturer is not worried for a different reason. It might expect plenty of pans to fail and still bet that few customers will bother to claim.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Look for an answer that closes that gap: a pan that does not work well or last long really would cost its manufacturer, because many buyers would seek reimbursement. Then a warranty can only sit on a pan the manufacturer expects to hold up.

Notice who the conclusion is talking to: a buyer who would never bother to claim. So the answer has to be about other buyers. Their claims are what make the warranty mean something.

notes.body:
A says most people who buy a pan with a warranty "would seek reimbursement" if it failed. Now follow the chain. If the pan were bad, many buyers would claim, the manufacturer would have to reimburse many customers, and by the premise it would not offer the warranty. So a pan with a warranty is one the manufacturer expects to work well and last. That is why even a buyer who would never claim should buy it.

The move: when a premise says a party avoids a cost, check what makes the cost real. Here the cost depends on buyers actually claiming, and A supplies that.

B compares pans only "at the time of purchase." The argument cares whether a pan will keep working and last long, which is what a warranty is supposed to signal. A pan can match the others on day one and still fail in a year. B also says nothing about why manufacturers offer warranties, so it does not connect the premise to the conclusion.

C ties price to warranties. It does not show that a warranty means a good pan. The conclusion already accepts paying more, so learning that pans with warranties tend to cost more adds no reason to buy them.

D ties price to quality. The conclusion says to buy pans with a warranty, not expensive pans. Even if the priciest pans last longest, that gives no reason to prefer a pan with a warranty over one without at the same price.

E says most warranties "provide for full customer satisfaction." That describes what a claim gets you. But the buyer in the conclusion would never make a claim, so the warranty's terms do not matter to them. E also does not explain why a manufacturer would avoid putting a warranty on a bad pan.

note: Evaluate kept a quoted paraphrase ("if they aren't worried...") that is not bank wording, plus casual "our author"; rewrote that step without invented quotation marks, everything else approved as written.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: A recent study found that in each of the last ten years, the number of traffic accidents that resulted in death was greater during the day than during the night.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: It is more dangerous for an individual to drive during the day than during the night.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The evidence counts fatal accidents: in each of the last ten years, more happened during the day than during the night. The conclusion is about risk to "an individual": driving by day is more dangerous for each driver.

Given that more fatal accidents happen by day, how could we still argue that night driving is just as dangerous? Count the drivers. If far more people drive during the day, the day could have more fatal accidents and still be safer per driver. A bigger total is not a bigger rate.

So the argument needs a reason the danger itself is higher during the day: something about daytime driving that raises the risk for each driver.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Four answers will strengthen by giving a day-specific risk: something that makes each daytime trip more dangerous, or each nighttime trip safer. The correct answer will not. Expect it to show no day-versus-night difference at all, so it cannot explain why the day is more dangerous.

notes.body: A gives a daytime-only hazard: only during the day do unsafe vehicles outnumber safe ones. Every daytime driver shares the road with more unsafe vehicles, so the higher daytime death count reflects real risk, not just more traffic. That strengthens.

B says there is less law enforcement during the day. Less enforcement plausibly means more reckless driving goes unchecked, which raises the risk for each daytime driver. That is a day-specific reason for the extra fatal accidents, so it strengthens.

C says people drive more cautiously at night. That makes each night trip safer than a day trip, which explains the extra daytime fatal accidents with something other than traffic volume. It strengthens.

D is the exception. More travelers per vehicle over the past ten years is a trend across day and night alike. It might raise deaths per accident, but nothing in D says the change hits daytime harder. Without a day-versus-night difference, it does nothing to show the day is more dangerous for an individual.

The move on a Strengthen EXCEPT built on a comparison: each strengthener has to favor one side of the comparison. An answer that applies equally to both sides cannot help.

E says people drive faster during the day than during the night. Higher speeds make crashes more likely and more deadly, so each daytime trip carries more risk than a night trip. That is another day-specific risk, so it strengthens.

note: E note said faster driving "applies only to daytime driving", but E is a relative claim (faster by day than by night); reworded that one sentence, rest approved.
